questions.question: What is a mode of a random variable $X$?
options: A value where the PMF or PDF attains its maximum

questions.question: For a discrete distribution, what does a mode maximize?
options: The cumulative distribution function at every point

questions.question: For a continuous distribution, what does a mode maximize?
options: The probability of a single exact value

questions.question: Can a distribution have more than one mode?
options: No, every distribution has exactly one mode
Only if it has no PMF or PDF
Yes, it may have several modes

questions.question: For continuous distributions, what warning applies to density height?
options: Density height is always a probability mass
Density height is not itself probability
Density height must be less than one
Density height is the CDF value

questions.question: What are the modes of a fair die distribution?
Where is the mode of a normal distribution?
If a PMF has probabilities $0.1,0.6,0.3$ at values $1,2,3$, what is the mode?
A mixture of two separated normal distributions can have how many modes?
If two discrete values both have the largest probability, what are they?
options: Only the smaller value is a mode
Only the larger value is a mode

questions.question: How is a mode different from a mean?
options: A mode is a most likely value; a mean is an average.
A mode is always the expected value
A mean always maximizes the density
A mode is defined only by squared deviations.

questions.question: Why can a fair die have every face as a mode?
options: The die has no probability mass function
The mode must equal the median
All faces tie for the maximum probability mass
Every face has probability greater than one

questions.question: Why should one be careful interpreting a continuous mode as 'most probable exact value'?
options: Point probabilities are zero for continuous RVs.

questions.question: If a density has equal highest peaks at $-2$ and $2$, what can be said?
options: It has two modes, at $-2$ and $2$.

questions.question: If a PMF assigns probabilities $0.4,0.4,0.2$ to $0,1,2$, what are the modes?
A density is highest at $x=5$ but $P(X=5)=0$. Is $5$ still a mode?
options: No, a mode needs positive point probability
No, continuous distributions cannot have modes.
Yes; it maximizes density, not point probability.

questions.question: A distribution's mode is its most probable value. Which situation gives 'no unique mode'?
options: The maximum may be attained at more than one value

questions.question: Why is the mode a shape-related summary?
options: It gives only the total probability.
It identifies peaks of the mass or density.
It is always equal to variance

questions.question: A student says a fair die has mode $3.5$ because that is its center. What is wrong?
options: The mode is a value of maximum probability mass.
The center is always the only mode
A fair die has no PMF
The mode must equal the expected value.

questions.question: If a continuous density is constant on $[0,1]$, what happens to the mode?
options: All points of $[0,1]$ attain the max density.
No point can maximize the density.
